notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Long white plates with the blue EU strip on the left.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Round, baton-like bollards with a rectangular reflector on the front and two round ones on the back, white or orange.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: The least consistent poles of the Baltics: round wooden poles with diagonal supports, square concrete ones, and trident tops with one insulator on top and two at the side.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Most wooden poles have a small metal cap on top, as in the Nordic countries.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Outer road lines sometimes consist of short dashes.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are red with white arrows, the reverse of the other two Baltic states.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue kilometre markers stand perpendicular to the road, with numbers on both sides.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Warning and speed signs have a thin red border running to the sign's edge, with no white outline.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Plain A-type guardrails without reflectors; the other Baltic states can have reflectors.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian signs have 3 stripes and a detailed figure with shoes and an attached head.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Bus stop signs show a bus with four windows, as in Lithuania; Latvia's has five.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue and white signpost wrappings are very common.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Direction signs are blue with white text and outline, the arrowhead's back edge vertical.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A Finnic language closely related to Finnish, with Ä, Ö, Ü and Õ with a tilde; the words for street and road are tänav and tee.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Oval blue house numbers are fairly common.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Wood and white brick, steep corrugated metal roofs and painted stone walls; wooden buildings are more common than in the other Baltics.

notes.subject: coverage
notes.text: Generation 3 often has a slight green tint over part of the panorama, called green blur.

notes.subject: coverage
notes.text: Generation 3 covers very thin rural roads more than in the other Baltics; use only as a last resort.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Fairly flat; only 10 percent is above 100 metres and the highest point is 318 metres.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The hilliest areas are in the southeast and the southern half of Lääne-Viru County.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: A large Russian minority gives bilingual signs with Cyrillic around Narva in the far northeast.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: The capital's old town is a near-perfect medieval and renaissance area that can resemble central European cities.

notes.subject: coverage
notes.text: A small island has only generation 4 coverage, shot in late autumn with fallen brown leaves and moody dark clouds near sunset.

notes.subject: coverage
notes.text: Near Tartu there is also plenty of autumn coverage, sometimes cloudy.
